MOFs-derived copper@nitrogen-doped carbon composite: the synergistic effects of N-types and copper on selective CO2 electroreduction
Yuan-Sheng Cheng, a Xin-Ping Chu, a Min Ling, b Na Li, b Kong-Lin Wu, b Fang-Hui Wu, a Hong Li, a Guozan Yuan, a and Xian-Wen Wei a, *
Development of Cu-based complex electrocatalysts is more easily to achieve a high activity and selectivity for reducing CO2 to multi-carbon hydrocarbons, exploring the synergistic effect between Cu and other materials may help the design of high efficient catalysts. This paper reports an impact factor for synergistic effect between Cu and nitrogen doped carbon (NC) support by comparing CO2 reduction reaction (CO2RR) performances on MOFs-derived copper@nitrogen-doped carbon (Cu-NC) catalysts obtained by calcination of N-containing benzimidazole modified Cu-BTC (1, 3, 5-benzenetricarboxylic acid) MOFs (BEN-Cu-BTC) at different temperatures. Different types of Cu-NC samples show the N species- and contentdependent catalysis for high selective electroreduction of CO2 to C2 products. The characterization and experimental results indicate that high contents of pyrrolic-N and Cu-N species formed at the annealing temperature of 400 °C can facilitate the C2-product generation on Cu surface, with the reaction rates and faradaic efficiencies (FEs) for ethylene and ethanol being rethylene = 5.38 μmol•m −2•s-1 (FE = 11.2 %) and rethanol = 8.83 μmol•m −2•s-1 (FE = 18.4 %) at -1.01 V (vs. reversible hydrogen electrode (RHE)), respectively, while excess graphitic-N and oxidized-N on the Cu surface cause a large of H2 evolution and a rapid decrease of the CO2RR activity. These may be due to the differences of adsorption and valence state on Cu-NC interactions. The results mean that the catalytic activity on MOFs-derived Cu-NC catalyst can be controlled by N-types changes dominating of annealing temperatures, offering a new tack for designing highly selective complex catalysts, since the electrocatalytic performance of the Cu-NC remains stable over 8 h.

sections.heading: Introduction
sections.text:
Directly fixing atmospheric CO2 and transmuting them into renewable energy (such as hydrocarbons and alcohols) to satisfy the rising global energy demands is regarded as a goal of future technologies. Electrolysis, which can be driven by solar energy, is a highly attractive way to meet this goal, due to its high efficiency and controllability. However, the strong competitive hydrogen evolution reaction (HER) and poor selectivity of complex CO2 reduction reaction (CO2RR) become the bottlenecks for electrochemical CO2RR development.1 Therefore, identifying and developing high performance electrocatalysts which can solve these problems is important but still remaining challenges. Among the present electrocatalysts, Cu based materials are considered to be one of the most promising electrocatalysts for CO2RR owing to its low
cost and high activity. Meanwhile, Cu is also the only known metal which can selectively reduce CO2 to hydrocarbons and alcohols.2-16 To meet the practical application and achieve the maximum reducing capability, Cu is usually hybridized with carbon materials to avoid aggregation and expose more catalytically active sites, including carbon black (CB),4 graphene,5,6 carbon nanotubes (CNTs) as well as metal−organic frameworks (MOFs)-derived porous carbon materials.4,17 Particularly, MOFs-derived carbon materials have attracted great attention recently because of their simple synthesis method, controllable elemental composition and porosity.18
Usually, through the thermal decomposition under inert atmosphere, the MOFs’ metal ions can be converted into metal,19,20 metal oxide,21-23 clusters or even single atoms,24 with organic ligands carbonization forming a carbon or heteroatoms doped carbon, which can provide an abundant active sites for CO2RR. 25 For example, ZIF-8 derived metal free nitrogendoped carbon (NC) can effectively convert CO2 to CO. 26 Additionally, through controlling calcination to form Cu cluster catalyst from HKUST-1 MOFs, the selectivity of multiplecarbon product generation is improved.7,10,11 The use of Cubased bimetallic systems has been proved to be a potential way to enhance the performance of current CO2 electroreduction systems for the production of alcohols or formate.9,13,14 However, rarely research reports the synergistic effect between both of them. surface of catalysts, the local fields around Cu play a not negligible role in CO2RR. 8 A typical example is that after assembled on the pyridinic-N rich graphene, 7 nm Cu nanoparticles (NPs) showed higher selectivity to ethylene than before.6 Therefore, to explore the synergistic effect and clarify the mechanism affecting between Cu and MOFs-derived nitrogen-doped carbon support is very essential for enhancing the reduction activity and selectivity of MOFs-derived catalysts.
In this work, a series of Cu NPs-NC catalysts were prepared by calcining N-containing benzimidazole (BEN) modified CuBTC (1, 3, 5-benzenetricarboxylic acid) MOFs (BEN-Cu-BTC) at different temperatures to explore the effects of N-doping on CO2RR. Electrochemical measurement results indicate that the existence of N-doped carbon support formed at low temperature significantly increases the CO2RR activity and selectivity to ethylene and ethanol. However, with the annealing temperature rising, the Faradaic efficiencies of CO2 reduction products are substantially suppressed but predominantly HER. Combining with the characterizations and controlled experimental results, we obtain that the types and contents of nitrogen atoms in carbon support can directly affect the CO2RR performance on the loading Cu NPs surface, and choosing an appropriate thermal temperature to optimize MOFs-derived carbon material composition for better use of synergic effect also merit attention.

sections.heading: Materials
sections.text: Nafion (5%, wt %) solution and Nafion N117 proton exchange membrane were obtained from Alfa Aesar. HCP-030 carbon paper was purchased from Toray Industries, Inc. Other reagents were obtained from Adamas reagent and used without further purification. The ultrapure water (18.2 MΩ*cm) supplied by Milli-Q system was used in whole experiment.

sections.heading: Preparation of catalysts
sections.text:
In brief, the BEN modified Cu-BTC was synthesized as previously reported with slight modifications.27 0.1 mmol Cu(NO3)2•3H2O and 9 mL mixture solvent of ethanol and N, N-
dimethylformamide (Vethanol: VDMF = 1 : 1) were added into a 50 mL round-bottom flask to form solution A. Similarly, 1.7mmol BEN was dissolved in another 9 mL mixture and designated as solution B. Then solution B was slowly injected into the solution A followed by 15 min stirring at 90 °C to obtain a light blue former solution C. After that, 0.1 mmol 1, 3, 5- benzotriacetic acid (BTC) was added into ethanol (9 mL)/DMF (9 mL) mixture to form a transparent solution D. Subsequently, Solution D was added to former solution C and stirred for 6 h at 90 °C. The BEN modified Cu-BTC MOFs was collected by centrifugation and washed with ethanol at least 6 times, and dried at 60 °C. The dried BEN-Cu-BTC MOFs were annealed at 200, 300, 350, 400, 600 and 800 °C for 1.5 h with a heating rate of 1 °C/min under Ar atmosphere, respectively. (Caution: An enough degassing time should be adopted to ensure that all the air adsorbed by the huge surface area MOFs was evacuated by pump). After cooling to room temperature, the Ar supply were stopped, and the flange cover were opened to let products slowly expose to air overnight for passivation treatment. After that, the black powders were collected, washed twice with water and dried at 60 °C, the final products were recorded as Cu-NC200, Cu-NC300, Cu-NC350, Cu-NC400, Cu-NC600 and Cu-NC800, respectively.
For comparison, the samples without nitrogen were prepared by the similar procedures except for directly adding the solution D into solution A and shunning use of BEN. The samples obtained are denoted as Cu-C400, Cu-C600 and Cu-C800 etc.. In addition, a different N species sample was obtained by expanding annealing time of BEN-Cu-BTC to 3 h at 400 °C, and recorded as Cu-NC400-3.

sections.heading: Electrochemical measurements
sections.text:
All the electrochemical measurements were conducted on a gas-tight H-type cell system (Fig. S1) at an electrochemical station (CHI 760D). The gas products were directly injected into gas chromatography (GC, 7820A, Agilent) for on-line detection. The liquid products were sampled and retained after the reaction, then detected by 1H NMR spectra (NMR, Avance HD 400, Bruker). sections.heading: Results and discussion
sections.text:
All of Cu-NC catalysts were synthesized by annealing the BEN (using as nitrogen sources) modified Cu-BTC MOFs at different temperatures (Scheme 1). TGA and XRD were employed to investigate the phase changes under thermal treatment. As shown in Fig. S4, only the weight percent of water or solvent in MOFs decreased until temperature up to 250 °C. Then, with the temperature rising, Cu2+ ions were gradually converted to Cu2O (JCPDS 78-2076) first and subsequently further be reduced to Cu (JCPDS 04-0836), corresponding to an abrupt mass loss in TGA (Fig. S4-6).27,28 When the temperature reached to 350 °C or even higher, only Cu peaks can be found while no obvious Cu2O peaks existence in Fig. 1a and Fig. S6, indicating that all MOFs metal nodes were completely converted to pure crystalline Cu phases, on the other hand, the mass loss between 350-450 °C was attributed to organic ligands carbonization.
Additional FT-IR and Raman spectra can further prove the carbonization process of MOFs organic ligands in Fig. S7. Upon treatment with calcining, several characteristic peaks of BTC ligand located at 1200-1700 cm-1 in FT-IR spectra (Fig. S7a) disappeared and were replaced by a new band at 1620 cm1 corresponding to ν(C=C) of graphitic domains.7 In addition, the Raman spectra of Cu-NC simples do not contain any signals except D band (~1360 cm-1) and G band (~1590 cm-1) associated with carbon structure (Fig. S7b), implying the organic ligands and Cu2+ ions were completely carbonized and reduced.29 The specific surface area changes of BEN-Cu-BTC before and after calcining were measured by N2 adsorptiondesorption isotherms. As shown in Fig. 1b, the SBET of CuNC400 (37 m2 g-1) is much smaller than that of initial BEN-CuBTC (711 m2 g-1), this may be because most of pores were blocked or broken by high temperature treatment.30
The morphologies and microscopic structures of asprepared samples were examined by SEM, TEM and HR-TEM observations. As shown in Fig. 2a-b, differ from original octahedral Cu-BTC (Fig. S8),31 the BEN modified Cu-BTC exhibits a well-defined solid cuboctahedral profiles with diameters of 400-600 nm. After pyrolysis under argon atmosphere, the cuboctahedral morphologies were well retained while many small nanoparticles were uniformly embedded in them (Fig. 2c-d). According to the statistics, the average sizes of Cu NPs obtained from different temperature samples, are about 28(±20), 34(±16) and 39(±21) nm for Cu-NC400, CuNC600 and Cu-NC800, respectively, which means that the sizes of Cu NPs are increasing with the annealing temperature rising (Fig. S9). HRTEM images in Fig. 2e-f clearly demonstrate that Cu NPs are embedded in carbon support with few layers of carbon shell covered on them and the observed lattice fringes of 0.18 nm can be assigned to the (200) planes of crystallite Cu.20,32 Moreover, HAADF-STEM and corresponding EDS mapping images (Fig. 2h) reveal that the loading Cu element is inserted in carbon matrix which includes C, N and O elements evenly distributing.
To further probe the chemical states of different annealed temperature Cu-NC samples, XPS was conducted. As shown in Fig. 3 and Fig. S10, C, N, O and Cu species were confirmed from XPS survey spectrum, which is also corresponded to the EDX result (Fig. S11). The high-resolution Cu 2p spectra exhibit two characteristic peaks of Cu 2p3/2 and Cu 2p1/2 from Cu0 or Cu+ located at 932.2 and 952.3 eV.27,33 No prominent Cu2+ or Cu2+ satellite peaks can be found in Cu 2p spectra, indicating that almost all the Cu2+ MOFs metal nodes have been reduced. In addition, Cu LMM X-ray-induced Auger peaks were tested to further differentiate between Cu0 and Cu+. As shown in Fig. 3c, Cu LMM spectrum of Cu-NC400 could be fitted into five peaks, two peaks located at 918.4 and 916.6 eV are characteristics of Cu(0) and Cu(I)-Ox/Nx, other three peaks at 913.5, 919.5 and 921.3 eV are the different transitions states of the Cu LMM spectrum.20,33-35 In addition, the same phenomenon was also observed in other sample (Fig. S12). Considering that the electron spectroscopy is a surface sensitive analysis, in combination with the results of XRD, Raman and HR-TEM, we proposed that the presence of Cu(I) species may attributed to Cu-N or/and Cu-O bonds on Cu@NC interfaces,20,35 not just the surface Cu oxidized by air during the storage period, since the BTC has the oxygen-containing

All the N 1s spectra can be fitted into at least five peaks at around 398.3, 399.0, 400.3, 401.3 and 403.5 eV, which are features of pyridinic-N, Cu−N, pyrrolic-N, graphitic-N and oxidized-N, respectively (Table S2).36,37 In comparison, the total nitrogen percentages decreases with the annealing temperature increasing, from the initial 5.25% in Cu-NC400 to 4.17 % and 3.20 % in Cu-NC600 and Cu-NC800, respectively. Besides, the composition of N types also changed in different samples, showing that the ratios of Cu−N and pyrrolic-N were decreased significantly, while graphitic-N and oxidized-N increases accordingly in higher temperature treatment samples. This might because of the instable nitrogen atoms were easily oxidized or lost while the stable nitrogen in carbon lattice were retained at high temperature, resulting in the contents increasing of graphitic-N and oxidized-N.26,38,39 In addition, high temperature also caused the increase of Cu NPs sizes, which reduce the Cu@NC interactions, leading to the Cu-N level decreased.
To explore the effects of different N-doping contents and types on the CO2RR, the CO2RR activities of as-prepared samples were evaluated in 0.1 M KHCO3 electrolyte using a typical three-electrode H-cell system. The cyclic voltammetry (CV) curves response of different samples were first given in Fig. 4a, revealing that Cu-NC400 have the largest current density, which means that it possesses the highest
electrocatalytic activity.37 Interestingly, the three different samples exhibited nearly the same electrochemical active surface areas (ECSA) (Fig. S13), but the extremely different catalytic results were obtained. For obtained Cu-NC catalysts, only three kinds of gas products (H2, CO and C2H4) can be found within the tested potential range and the corresponding FEs were given in Fig. 4b-d. As the results clearly show, CuNC800 exhibits a strong competitive HER, particularly at –1.11 V (versus RHE) the maximum FEH2 of 78.7% is achieved, with a poor activity for CO2RR (total FEs for CO2RR gas products are below 5 % at all range), which may be due to the high content of graphitic-N (10.6 ‰) and oxidized-N (4.4 ‰) enhance the H* adsorption on Cu surface.40,41 For other lower annealed temperature samples, both FECO and FEC2H4 values are all well above the Cu-NC800. Besides, 400 °C was proved to be the optimal annealed temperature to obtain the sample for the formation of ethylene, and the corresponding FEC2H4 values of Cu-NC400 gradually increased with increasing of negative potentials. Additionally, the FECO of Cu-NC400 stably maintains over 20 % at the range from –0.81 to –1.11 V (versus RHE), and the Cu-NC400 displays the smallest Tafel slope (Fig. 4e) for CO production (132 mV dec-1) comparing to Cu-NC600 (179 mV dec-1) and Cu-NC800 (291 mV dec-1), which suggested that Cu-NC400 have the rapidest kinetic activity, on the other hand, the Tafel slope is closed to theoretical value (118 mV dec-1), indicated that the rate-determining step (RDS) is the transformation of first electron from CO2 to CO2 • − intermediate (Fig. S14).42,43 Notably, although initial BEN-CuBTC reveals a well catalytic activity to CO production, the poor

The liquid products of formate and ethanol were detected by 1H-NMR (Fig. S16). As for Cu-NC400, the FEs values for liquid products are all above 20% under applied potentials, and attained 18.4% for CH3CH2OH (rethanol = 8.83 μmol•m −2•s-1) and 7.2% for formate (rformate = 20.73 μmol•m −2•s-1) at –1.01 V (versus RHE, optimum potential with the highest CO2RR activity), respectively, which are higher than many MOF based Cu catalysts reported before (Table S3).7,9-14
To attain more insight into the role of N-doping in CO2RR, the similar samples without nitrogen doped were synthesized and examined as controls. The average sizes of Cu NPs in CuC400, Cu-C600 and Cu-C800 are about 26 (±22), 28 (±21) and 33 (±30) nm, respectively, indicated that the higher annealing temperature lead to the larger sizes of Cu NPs (Fig.S17). As shown in Fig. 4g, the CO2RR performances of different samples are closely related to the nitrogen atoms but much more H2 were produced for the samples obtained at lower temperature. In the controlled Cu-C samples without nitrogen, the gas products of CO2RR are CO, C2H4 and CH4, but the total FE values are limited to only 15%, which are much less than the Cu-NC samples except for Cu-C800. The XAES and XPS spectra were used to compare the Cu valence changes in CuNC400 and Cu-C400 samples, respectively. The Cu LMM results indicate that Cu(I) species in Cu-NC sample is harder to be reduced to Cu0 under CO2RR (Fig. S18), since after 2 h of CO2RR, the Cu + ratio decreased from 67 % to 59 % in CuNC400, while from 45 % to 23 % in Cu-C400. Additionally, comparing to the amounts and changes between Cu-N (399.0 eV) and Cu-O (531.2 eV) species27 in different samples (Fig. S19), the results show that the Cu(I) species in Cu-NC400 sample preferring to form the Cu(I)-N species, and the Cu(I)-N species is more stable than Cu(I)-O species. A possible reason is that according to the Hard-Soft-Acid-Base principle, the softsoft Cu(I)-N-donor linkers is easier to form and achieving a higher stability than soft-hard Cu(I)-carboxyl linkers.44 As suggested by literatures, Cu+ is already to be proved as the active sites and can boost the C2-product generation. 15,16 For the investigation of the influence of Cu size, the control sample was also obtained by increasing the annealing time to 3 h under 400 °C. As shown in Fig. S20, the Cu-NC400-3 has the similar total N content (3.4%) and Cu size (41(±26)nm) to those of CuNC800, but exhibits a much better catalytic activity to CO2RR (FEs: CO 18.6%, C2H4 9.3%, CH4 3.1% , ethanol 15.2%, formate 16.5% and H2 34.6%, at –1.01 V versus RHE) than that of Cu-NC800 (FEs: CO 1.9%, C2H4 0.95%, formate 30.4% and H2 62.5%). The possible explanation for this result is that the Cu-NC400-3 has higher pyrrolic-N content (13.7‰) than that of Cu-NC800 (7.6‰). In addition, although Cu-NC600 has the similar pyrrolic-N content (12.2‰) and even higher Cu-N content (10.9‰) than that Cu-NC400-3, the high content graphitic-N (7.6‰) and oxidized-N (2.4‰) enhanced the competitive HER (FEH2=55.2%) leading to the decrease of CO2RR activity.
From the above results, we proposed that the synergistic effect between Cu and the N atoms doped in carbon support play the main role in CO2RR performance changes. Among
them, the positive effects achieve a high CO2RR activity and increase the selectivity to ethylene and ethanol. For this result, a reasonable explanation is that the electronegative N atoms hog electrons from the adjacent carbon atoms, assigning positively charged carbon atoms to serve as Lewis base sites and further increasing the adsorption of CO2 on Cu-NC surface, which helps increase the activity of CO2RR. 45-47 Additionally, high content N doped in carbon shell also helps to stabilize the Cu+ species on Cu-NC interactions, which is also promoted the C–C coupling reaction, exhibiting a high selectivity to ethylene and ethanol. However, the dominant graphitic-N and oxidized-N show a strong adsorption of H* resulting in a predominantly HER.41 Another inescapable impact is that with the coating of NC shell, Cu-NC catalyst not only can accelerate the RDS step but also reveals an excellent stability,5 which can work stable at least 8 h without any attenuation (Fig. 4h).

sections.heading: Conclusions
sections.text: In summary, for MOFs-derived Cu catalysts, the N contents and types in carbon shell play an inescapable impact in electrocatalytic CO2RR performance. The high contents of pyrrolic-N and Cu-N doped in carbon support provide abundant CO2 adsorption sites and also facilitate the carbon–carbon coupling reactions on Cu surface, showing a high selectivity for ethylene and ethanol product generation. However, not all types of nitrogen atoms play the active effects; excessive contents of graphitic-N and oxidized-N atoms will lead to a strong HER competition. Therefore, optimizing the N structure is necessary to achieve a better synergy between Cu and NC support. In short, this work offers an approach to explore and design high performance Cu-based catalysts, and can be extended to other fields, such as oxygen reduction, N2 reduction and so on.
